newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels see progress in hostage crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels see progress in hostage crisis talks.

text.p: The Marxist guerrilla group holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home said on Monday talks to end the siege were progressing because the government had realised the only solution was to negotiate.

With talks deadlocked since early March, President Alberto Fujimori has come under growing pressure to quickly find a peaceful outcome to the 97-day crisis, Isaac Velazco, the rebels' international spokesman, told Reuters.
"The greatest achievement in the last 15 to 20 days has been the government's recognition that the only solution is through negotiation," Velazco said by telephone from Germany.
"The government does not have much time as it liked to claim earlier. It is now under a lot of pressure from abroad -- particularly from Japan."

President Alberto Fujimori has said throughout the standoff he is patient enough to wait months for a peaceful solution. But there are growing signs he is willing to make some concessions to speed up negotiations.

A Peruvian newspaper reported on Monday that the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) may be offered a multi-million dollar ransom, asylum in the Caribbean and the release of some of its jailed comrades in return for freeing the hostages.
The proposal was drawn up by the three-man guarantors commission overseeing the stalled talks and would be presented to the government and the rebels "in coming days," the daily La Republica said.
MRTA spokesman Velazco said the offer was "feasible, could be studied and lead to a solution to the crisis as long as it considers the freedom of our jailed fighters and leaders."
Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa has made a formal proposal to the government detailing which prisoners the group wants freed, Velazco added. He did not elaborate.

Since the rebels stormed the diplomatic residence and seized hundreds of hostages on Dec. 17, they have publicly insisted on the release of up to 450 jailed comrades. But MRTA members have also said a reduced number of releases could be negotiated as long as those freed were high-ranking comrades.
Ongoing visits by a guarantors sub-committee to jailed MRTA members have raised speculation the government was compiling a list of rebels it might be prepared to release.
Tokyo also suggested this sort of behind-the-scenes work was pushing the crisis closer to a solution, despite the sides holding only one face-to-face meeting in more than two weeks.

"The situation may appear deadlocked at first sight, but I am convinced that the issue is heading towards a solution," Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura told reporters in Tokyo on Monday. "I think the time is ripe for a peaceful settlement."
Komura was just back from a trip to discuss the crisis with Fujimori in Lima and secure formal agreements from Cuba and the Dominican Republic to give the hostage-takers asylum if the MRTA agreed.
The guerrillas have reserved comment on seeking asylum, but Velazco said it would be acceptable if it was part of a deal to free prisoners.

"If the unit (at the residence) and our prisoners have to leave the country for there to be a solution to the crisis, we have no problem with that," he said. "We will know when the time is right to return."

With the acceptance of a possible asylum, members of the guarantors commission continued their efforts on Monday to find further common ground between the parties to be able to relaunch face-to-face negotiations.

Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig met with the rebels inside the besieged house while the Vatican representative, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, held a separate meeting with Fujimori at the presidential palace.

Early in the crisis the rebels freed most of their VIP hostages. They have held onto their most powerful bargaining chips, including Fujimori's younger brother, two government ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, as well as two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
